title: The memory hierarchy: the stored-program idea, and the latency numbers that follow from it

claims.text: John von Neumann circulated the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC from the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at the University of Pennsylvania on 30 June 1945. It described a machine holding both its instructions and its data in the same addressable memory, from which a control unit fetches and decodes them in sequence.

source.title: John von Neumann, First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, 30 June 1945

claims.text: ENIAC, built at the same school, was programmed by setting switches and plugging cable connections between its units, so changing the computation it performed was a physical rewiring task rather than the loading of a new set of stored instructions.

source.title: ENIAC — programming by setting switches and plugging cable connections, Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania

claims.text: The widely circulated latency table compiled by Jeff Dean, originally by Peter Norvig, gives: L1 cache reference 0.5 ns; branch mispredict 5 ns; L2 cache reference 7 ns; mutex lock and unlock 25 ns; main memory reference 100 ns, described in the table itself as 200x L1; read 4K randomly from SSD 150,000 ns; read 1 MB sequentially from memory 250,000 ns; round trip within the same datacenter 500,000 ns; disk seek 10,000,000 ns, described as 20x a datacenter round trip; read 1 MB sequentially from disk 20,000,000 ns; and send a packet from California to the Netherlands and back 150,000,000 ns.

source.title: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know — compiled by Jeff Dean, originally by Peter Norvig; the widely circulated gist, whose values date from around 2012 and whose forks and comments record later revisions

claims.text: The table's figures date from around 2012 and drift with hardware generation, which its forks and comment thread record: later revisions give register access about 0.3 ns, L1 about 1 ns, branch mispredict about 3 ns, L2 about 4 ns, L3 about 15 ns and main memory about 80 ns, and readers note that current solid-state drives are faster than the listed figure. The durable content is therefore the ratios rather than the values.

source.title: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know — compiled by Jeff Dean, originally by Peter Norvig; the widely circulated gist, whose values date from around 2012 and whose forks and comments record later revisions

beats.broke: storage was reasoned about as a single thing called memory, so code was written as though reaching any of it cost the same, and the arithmetic units spent their time waiting
beats.fix: treat the hierarchy as the design input: each level is orders of magnitude slower than the one above it, so the question for any operation is which level it touches and how often
beats.cost: the ratios are what matter and the absolute figures go stale, so the table has to be re-derived for the hardware in front of you rather than quoted
beats.interview: the latency numbers, and what they dictate about indexing and caching
